- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 2–5% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior period), model tends to overcorrect; reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 5–7 days.  
- If official supply net is negative and sentiment is bearish, model often underestimates downside; add 3–8% downward bias to forecast mean.  
- When sentiment swings from bullish to bearish within 3–5 days, model fails to adjust; apply a 5–10% downward correction to forecast mean.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if recent 18-day history shows high volatility or mean reversion, reduce forecast slope by 10–15% to avoid overfitting.  
- If official events are frequent and supply net is negative, model tends to overestimate bullishness; apply a 5–10% downward adjustment to forecast mean.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated bearish spikes (e.g., -0.5 to -1.0) and model ignores them, reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 7 days.  
- For 30-day forecasts with low historical volatility, model often underestimates downside; add 3–7% downward bias if sentiment is bearish.  
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows sharp decline, reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, model tends to overestimate bullishness; reduce forecast by 3–7% to align with sentiment.
